newsitem.title: MOROCCO: King Hassan reshuffles Moroccan cabinet.
newsitem.headline: King Hassan reshuffles Moroccan cabinet.

text.p: Moroccan King Hassan reshuffled the government of Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali on Wednesday night and replaced 20 ministers by a group of technocrats, a Moroccan senior official said.

"His majesty King Hassan replaced 20 ministers affiliated to political parties, including the justice and finance ministers. Four women were newly appointed as secretaries of state, for the first time since Moroccan independence in 1956," a palace senior official said.
Nawal al-Moutawakil, gold medalist in the 400 metre hurdles at the Los Angeles Olympic games in 1984, was named secretary of state for youth and sports, he added.
Filali, who is also foreign minister and has no political affiliation, remained in his post, the official said.

The king met the new government team after the reshuffle at the royal palace of Skhirat, 30 km (20 miles) south of Rabat, the official said, adding that a detailed government list would be released later.
The handover of office is expected for Friday because Thursday is a public holiday.
Earlier this month the Moroccan monarch told members of the government who belonged to political parties that he preferred they step down ahead of any election campaign.
Addressing a council of ministers at Skhirat palace, the king said then that under the constitution they could remain in office but he judged it better they did not.

"Despite the constitution allowing them to remain in government while leading electoral campaigns, his Majesty judged it preferable from a moral viewpoint that...they should devote themselves entirely to their political and partisan activity," the official MAP news agency reported.
The present government led by Filali was appointed in February 1995 although Filali has held his position and the post of foreign minister since November 1993.
A dozen ministers, including Interior Minister Driss Basri, also have no party ties and will remain in place to supervise parliamentary elections expected in September.

"After September elections, the 330-seat parliament will hold its autumn session in October as scheduled and without delay," a parliament spokesman said commenting on rumours in political circles of a possible delay to the legislative elections.
Under the constitution, the Chamber of Representatives would hold its autumn session on the second Friday of October.

Last June, Morocco held local elections for 1,547 councils as part of a series of ballots to culminate in September with a general election for a new lower house of parliament and later for the upper house.
